title: Projections of extreme rainfall in South Africa using CMIP6 ISIMIP models
abstract: The escalating impacts of climate change pose a significant risk to South Africa’s water resources and infrastructure, particularly as a result of increased frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall. This study presents extreme rainfall projections for the country by analysing Phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP) global climate models (GCMs) from 2020 to 2100, under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. Five models and their ensembles were evaluated against ECMWF ERA5-Land and station data using Taylor diagrams, NSE, RMSE, PBIAS, and R². The ensemble outperformed individual models, which showed a similar spatial bias, underestimating rainfall over the escarpment while overestimating it in the lowlands. Rainfall changes were analysed for the near- (2020–2055) and far-future (2065–2100), focusing on the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles. Future midlatitude and subtropical circulation changes were projected to intensify the west-east rainfall gradient, leading to a drier west and a wetter east. This trend drives an overall increase in extreme rainfall events across South Africa. Annually, this is reflected in drier conditions projected along the coast and northeast in the far-future (5th and 50th percentiles), while the eastern half will likely experience increased extreme wet conditions (95th percentile). January projects rainfall increases in the eastern interior, with extreme wet conditions increasing by 35–45 mm across scenarios. Conversely, October may experience increased extreme dry conditions (5th percentile), with more than 48 mm decrease in the far-future under SSP5-8.5. During austral summer (DJF), pronounced wet and dry extremes are projected over eastern South Africa. Austral winter (JJA) will likely experience persistent and intensifying dry and wet extremes along the coast, with the southwest Cape particularly vulnerable to severe dry conditions. Heavy rainfall days are projected to increase in eastern South Africa, exceeding 10 days in the eastern interior. This study is crucial for understanding rainfall extremes under a changing atmospheric circulation and unpins more effective climate change adaptation strategies in South Africa.
problem: Existing climate models struggle to reliably project regional rainfall in South Africa, particularly over complex terrain, due to coarse resolutions and inadequate representation of local atmospheric processes, resulting in significant projection uncertainties.
method: This study projects future extreme rainfall in South Africa by analyzing a multi-model ensemble of five CMIP6 ISIMIP models, focusing on changes in the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles for near- and far-future periods under two emission scenarios.
task: The task is to project future extreme rainfall events in South Africa by analyzing bias-adjusted and downscaled CMIP6 ISIMIP global climate models under low and high emission scenarios.
innovation: This paper leverages an ensemble of high-resolution CMIP6 ISIMIP models to project future extreme rainfall in South Africa, identifying an intensifying west-east rainfall gradient that results in a drier west and a wetter east with more frequent extreme events.

South Africa has experienced numerous catastrophic floods, primarily driven by storms and excessive rainfall, resulting in significant impacts on the environment, infrastructure, socioeconom- ics, and resource management. These have largely not been exclusively attributed to climate change, but have also been linked to human-induced land-use change (Mohomi 2022; Mohomi et al. 2024), and complex large-scale and remote atmospheric phenomena. The rainfall over much of South Africa is characterized by strong seasonality that is caused by seasonal shifts in the Hadley Cell and the tropical rain belt (Chikoore and Jury 2010).

In recent years, several rainfall-producing systems have triggered extraordinary heavy rainfall events, leading to sig- nificant impacts across South Africa. For example, floods caused by tropical cyclones Idai in March and Kenneth in April 2019 resulted in substantial lives lost and were among the most severe in southern Africa (Bopape et al. 2021).

A tropical-extratropical cloud band in February 2019 resulted in approximately 300 mm/4 h, which flooded a shopping mall in northeastern South Africa (Chikoore et al. 2021).

A severe flood occurred in the country's eastern KwaZulu- Natal (KZN) Province in April 2022, driven by a COL, a frequent feature over southern Africa. The extreme, spatially variable rainfall was caused by a crucial triple mesoscale interaction along the coast involving a coastal meso-low, a mesoscale convective system (MCS), and an intensively strengthened low-level wind jet across the northern Agul- has Current (Blamey and Reason 2009, 2012; Morake et al. 2021; Thoithi et al. 2022). These interactions were inten- sified by a low-level onshore jet that enhanced moisture flux convergence and uplift, producing the extreme rainfall that claimed the lives of at least 448 individuals, displaced 40,000 individuals, and affected 4,000 homes (ECHO 2022; Thoithi et al. 2022).

Climate change has also altered hydroclimatic extreme events, such as floods, droughts, heatwaves, and fire regimes (Mbokodo et al. 2020; Ranasinghe et al. 2021; Chikoore et al. 2021; Chikoore and Jury 2021; Singo et al. 2023), with impacts that may include regional or local environmental hazards, disturbed ecosystems, declining agricultural yield, water and food supply shortages, com- promised human health and health management, and flood control (Chikoore et al. 2021; Munyai et al. 2021).
